schools.summary: Gill lists everything Zophar disregards in order to begin, the distressed condition Job was in, his request for pity, his confession of faith and his advice that they cease persecuting him, and says he starts up with as much heat and passion as ever, still representing Job as a wicked man and a hypocrite.

Ellicott marks the escalation in manner as well as matter, a retort of greater vehemence in a more ornate style on the same burden; Keil and Delitzsch report that all modern expositors take the second verse as an apology for what follows, canvass the elliptical reading and Ewald defence of it, and then refuse the result as furnishing no acceptable meaning, rejecting Schultens sense of a disturbance of mind as too remote from Hebrew usage.

Henry describes the entry closely, that Zophar was displeased Job talked so like a good man, broke in upon him and began abruptly, taking no notice of what was said to move pity or evidence integrity and fastening on the reproof at the close.

Clarke calls Zophar the most inveterate of them all and says we must cease to call these men friends, relays Good rendering about the tumult that would transport him, and remarks that this is all the modesty the discourse contains; Wesley reads it as haste, that he speaks sooner than he intended and possibly interrupted Job mid-discourse.

debates.question: Can the second verse be construed at all?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch report the consensus reading it as an apology and the majority treating the preposition as elliptical, with Ewald defending its standing alone, then hold that in spite of this the verse furnishes no meaning that can be accepted and reject the proposed sense of a disturbance of mind as too remote from Hebrew usage; Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley all render it without visible difficulty, Clarke through Good, Ellicott as simple eagerness, Wesley as haste.

outliers.view: Refuses to call the three men friends at all, holding that Zophar sets no bounds to his invective and outrages every rule of charity, and that a man of so bitter a spirit must in general have been very unhappy.
Notes that the escalation is stylistic as well as moral, Zophar assuming a more ornate and elaborate manner while reiterating the same burden of the speedy doom of the wicked.

themes: then answered Zophar the Naamathite
my thoughts cause me to answer
the haste that interrupts
an apology for what follows
a verse that yields no meaning

schools.summary: Gill takes the check to be Job warning that they should beware of the sword, and reports that some understand Zophar to be claiming a divine oracle of the kind Eliphaz alleged earlier, so that being divinely furnished he thought it his duty to deliver it.

Clarke offers two referents for the reproach and concludes that Zophar assumes his old ground and retracts nothing, being determined to believe his judgment infallible; Wesley takes the speaker at his word, that he speaks not from passion but from certain knowledge.

Ellicott renders it as a reproof that puts him to shame and reads the next clause literally, that out of his understanding his spirit answers him, so that he professes an impulse within which he cannot but obey.

Henry refuses the profession, observing that the abundance of the heart is what the mouth speaks while Zophar fathers the instigation on the spirit of his understanding, and that men often mistake the dictates of their passion for the dictates of their reason.

Gregory reads the whole opening as a mind shaken by the terribleness of the last Judgment rather than a temper roused, and is clear that the friends erred by being uninstructed in the estimate of God judgments.

debates.question: Is the answer reason or passion?
debates.positions: Wesley takes Zophar at his word that he speaks not from passion but certain knowledge; Ellicott reports the claim neutrally as a professed impulse that must be obeyed; Henry denies it outright, that the spirit of the understanding should cause us to answer but whether it did so here is a question, since men mistake passion for reason and therefore think they do well to be angry; Gill notes that some take the claim further still, as a pretension to a divine oracle.

outliers.view: Reads the confusion of thought as the effect of seeing the terribleness of the last Judgment, since the mind spreads wider the more it considers what threatens it, and is transported diverse ways as it weighs by turns the evil done and the good left undone.

Diagnoses the friends error precisely, that though long acquaintance with Job life had taught them how to live well, they were uninstructed in forming an exact estimate of God judgments and would not believe the righteous could suffer here below.

Draws the maxim the exchange illustrates, that the best counsel is too often ill taken from an antagonist and may therefore be well spared, and that the friends had spirits too high to deal with a man in his low condition.

themes: the check of my reproach
the spirit of my understanding
passion mistaken for reason
a claim to a divine oracle
a mind shaken by judgment

schools.summary: Gill takes the appeal to antiquity as a taunt and adds the obvious qualification that Job could not have known it from so early, being comparatively of yesterday; he declines to grant the maxim even in its reduced form, since it may be true in many instances but is not invariable and without exception the case; and he presses the figure of the dung to its end from ancient burial usage.

Clarke reads the second clause literally as since Adam was placed on the earth, turns the verse back on the speaker, keeps the first man as the reference for the height as well, and hears in the seventh verse a hint that Zophar disbelieves the resurrection Job had just asserted.
Ellicott summarises the claim exactly, that the destruction of the wicked is affirmed to be not only certain but speedy.
Henry sorts the speech into heads, treating the doctrine as introduced by an appeal to what all mankind is supposed to know.
Wesley reduces the height to its plainest sense, advancement to great dignity and authority.

debates.question: Is the maxim about the wicked true as stated?
debates.positions: Ellicott reports it without endorsement as a claim of certain and speedy destruction; Gill traces how the friends retreated to it, having begun by denying the wicked ever prospered, and then refuses even the reduced version, that it may be true in many instances but is not invariable and without exception the case; Clarke turns it back on Zophar, that such is his character he has little reason to anticipate the day of judgment with joy.

debates.question: Does the seventh verse deny the resurrection?
debates.positions: Clarke suspects that Zophar hints his disbelief in the resurrection of the body which Job had solemnly asserted in the preceding chapter, or else held that the wicked are annihilated and the righteous only raised, a doctrine he says no scripture confirms; Gill, taking the perishing to reach the soul in eternity as well as the body in the grave, reads it as everlasting ruin rather than annihilation.

outliers.view: Supports the comparison to dung from ancient usage, that dead bodies were reckoned as dung and that the Arabians buried even their kings in dunghills.
Judges the verse as much by its temper as its doctrine, calling it a speech that partakes as much of the malevolence as of the asperity of Zophar spirit.

themes: knowest thou not this of old
the triumphing of the wicked is short
though his excellency mount up to the heavens
he shall perish for ever like his own dung
a maxim that will not hold

schools.summary: Gill offers both senses of the dream, one forgotten and irrecoverable and one remembered but illusory as a hungry man dreaming he eats; he explains the children courting the poor after the man death so as to escape reproach or revenge or a suit, notes that Jarchi renders it otherwise, and takes the bones literally of youthful sin and its bodily aftermath while recording that some read the word as secret sins.

Clarke hears the dream verse as a continued denial of the resurrection Job asserted, reads the next as reducing the children to servants of the poor, gives two further renderings from Good and Calmet, and prefers the sense of hidden things for the bones, naming Rosenmuller and German critics and Good for it while reporting that the Syriac, Arabic and Targum read the line as bones full of marrow; Wesley takes the bones for the whole body and the sin for the punishment of it.

Ellicott adds a fourth rendering of the tenth verse, that the poor may be said to oppress his children, and takes the disputed word in the eleventh for youthful vigour rather than sin, so that a man in the full vigour of life shall yet lie down with it in the dust.
Henry, sorting the speech into heads, files the clause under the lusts of the flesh, those being the sins to which that age is most tempted.

debates.question: How should the tenth verse be rendered?
debates.positions: Clarke says outright that the clause is variously translated and gives three versions beside the received one, that the children become servants to the poor, that his branches are involved in his iniquity so that the children suffer on his account, and that his own hands render to himself the evil he did to others; Gill keeps the received sense of courting the favour of the oppressed and notes a further reading in Jarchi; Ellicott adds that it may be turned around so that the poor oppress his children.

debates.question: What are his bones full of?
debates.positions: Gill reads literal youthful sin whose effect is the rotting of flesh and bone; Clarke prefers the sense of hidden things, so that secret vices bring down his strength, and names supporters for it while reporting three versions that read marrow instead; Ellicott takes the word for youthful vigour and not for sin at all; Wesley reads the sin as the punishment of it.

outliers.view: Illustrates the depth of the poverty by the curse upon Ham, a servant of servants, and notes that there are cases where the poor actually serve the poor, which he calls the most abject state of poverty there is.

Presses the dream figure to the waking, that the man who dreams he eats and drinks awakes empty and not at all refreshed, what he fancied being fled and never having had existence but in his imagination.

themes: he shall fly away as a dream
his children shall seek to please the poor
his bones are full of the sin of his youth
a clause variously translated
vigour that lies down in the dust

schools.summary: Gill judges from the context that covetousness is meant and reports Broughton rendering the word as wrong, while allowing a general application; he reads the sparing not as eating little but as valuing much, sin being a wicked man own child; and he presses the comparison of sin to bread of deceit that proves ashes and gravel stones.

Clarke refers the sweetness to the secret sins of the preceding verse and sets out the whole allegory of a man who takes poison for food and will scarcely let it down; Wesley gives the epicure with a morsel rolled about the mouth, and grades the bitterness in three steps from gall to the poison of asps that kills without remedy.

Henry files it under the forbidden pleasures of sense and offers two senses of the hiding, obstinate persistence in sin and the re-acting of it by memory, or a hypocrite industrious concealment of a beloved lust.

Ellicott suspects a target rather than a category, that the portrait of a gourmand aimed at Job was a fresh instance of heartless cruelty and of unfitness for the office of judge Zophar assumed; Keil and Delitzsch, rendering this run of verses, reach outside Scripture to the golden age of which the poets sang, when rivers of milk and nectar ran.

debates.question: What is the wickedness that is sweet in his mouth?
debates.positions: Gill judges from the context that it is covetousness or riches unlawfully got, citing Broughton rendering of the word as wrong, while allowing a general sense; Clarke refers it to the secret sins of the preceding verse; Henry files it under the lusts of the flesh; Ellicott suspects it is aimed at Job wealth, extracted from the bare fact of his having been rich.

debates.question: What does hiding it under the tongue signify?
debates.positions: Henry offers two and chooses neither, obstinate persistence in sin, since the man spares what he should kill and mortify, and the re-acting of the sin by revolving it in memory, or else a hypocrite concealment of his beloved lust to save the credit of his profession; Wesley reads an epicure keeping a morsel to prolong the pleasure; Clarke reads poison held for its sweetness; Gill reads the sparing of a beloved child.

outliers.view: Turns the portrait back on the speaker, holding that if the picture of a gourmand was meant for Job it showed heartless cruelty, an entire want of discernment of character, and unfitness for the office of judge Zophar was so ready to assume.
Reads the sparing of the morsel as the sparing of a beloved child, as Saul spared Agag and as a man spares an only son, sin being a wicked man own offspring and therefore dear to him.

themes: wickedness sweet in his mouth
he hide it under his tongue
his meat in his bowels is turned
the gall of asps within him
rivers of milk and nectar

schools.summary: Gill keeps the swallowing strictly to the figure, the riches being another man property devoured as food, and argues from the tense that the poison is not the sin but the punishment of it, noting that execution by the poison of asps was a penalty some peoples actually inflicted; he also takes the denial of rivers first as the thirst that poison excites.

Clarke supplies the physiology the vomiting image depends on and reads the poison the other way, as the besetting sin acting on the soul as venom on the body, citing the older belief that the venom lay in the gall; he then relays Good account of honey and butter as the yield of a rich pasturage and sets beside it a shelf of classical parallels from Pindar, Virgil, Ovid and Horace; Wesley states the loss plainly.

Ellicott draws a consequential inference from the language of milk and honey, that since the phrase is not precisely identical with the promise made of Canaan it may show a community of proverbial speech and need not have originated with the Pentateuch.

debates.question: Is the poison the sin or its punishment?
debates.positions: Gill argues from the tense that it cannot be the sin, which would have required a past or present form as though the wickedness were sucked in like milk, and reads it as the punishment instead; Clarke reads it the other way without qualification, that the delicious morsel and easily besetting sin acts on the life of the soul exactly as the poison of an asp acts on the body.

outliers.view: Cites the old naturalist for the placing of the venom, whether in the teeth or as a yellow liquor in the gums, and repeats his account of the asps in copulation and the young that eat out the mother belly.

Collects four classical parallels for the rivers of honey and butter, from a poet comparing his own song to milk and honey through to the golden age with its floods of milk and nectar and honey distilling from oaks.

themes: he hath swallowed down riches
he shall suck the poison of asps
the brooks of honey and butter
poison in the gall
a proverb older than the promise

schools.summary: Clarke prefers a reading from the Arabic supported by the Syriac, gives Good version and explains how it is reached, sets Houbigant against both and exclaims at how the doctors disagree, then commends Coverdale; on the next verse he renders the charge as the breaking in pieces of the forsaken of the poor and supplies a scene of famine orphans left to perish; and he takes the word rendered belly in its wider sense of the whole trunk and so of the thoughts seated there; Wesley leaves the construction alone and reads compensation for wrongs.

Keil and Delitzsch object on syntax rather than lexicon, refusing the translation that has him give back what he gained without swallowing it and rejecting every attempt to attach the last phrase to the first, since such readings run against the relative independence of the separate lines this poet preserves; Ellicott offers his own alternative and then answers the accusation of the next verse instead of expounding it.

Gill notes that the verse explains in words what vomiting had expressed in figure, refuses to soften the charge into the desertion of former dependents, and canvasses three senses of the want of quietness before deciding for punishment rather than sin.

debates.question: How should the eighteenth verse be rendered?
debates.positions: Clarke prefers an Arabic reading supported by the Syriac, that he shall return to labour and not eat, then gives Good version making a dearth his recompense, then Houbigant quite different one, before exclaiming at the disagreement and commending Coverdale sense; Keil and Delitzsch reject the syntactic basis of several of these and argue from the independence of the verse lines; Ellicott allows the latter part is probably right but offers his own alternative.

debates.question: Is the want of quietness his sin or his punishment?
debates.positions: Gill canvasses happiness in children, satisfaction in substance, and a restless craving that would make it his sin, then decides for punishment, that he has no quiet in his conscience because of how his riches were got; Clarke makes it endless dissatisfaction, an unending desire after secular good; Ellicott turns the clause into the cause rather than the effect, that because he knew no quietness within he shall save nothing of what he desires.

outliers.view: Breaks off from the exposition to exclaim at how the doctors disagree, having set four renderings of a single verse against one another.
Answers the accusation instead of expounding it, saying flatly that for these insinuations there was not a vestige of ground and that Job formally rebuts them later in the book.

themes: that which he laboured for shall he restore
he hath oppressed and forsaken the poor
a house which he builded not
no quietness in his belly
four renderings of one verse

schools.summary: Gill offers three senses of the twenty-first verse, nothing left in the belly, a table so mean that no crumb falls from it, and no heir left for his substance; and he lists the ways fulness turns to straitness before preferring the sharpest, a sudden dispossession in the height of prosperity as befell Nebuchadnezzar.

Ellicott reverses the twenty-first verse entirely, that nothing was left which he did not devour and therefore his prosperity shall not endure, and reads the hands that fall on him as the hands of the miserable in retaliation; Keil and Delitzsch read the clause about filling as introducing what follows, that to fill an insatiable belly God sends forth his glowing wrath and rains it into the man very flesh.

Clarke calls the paradox of the twenty-second verse a fine saying few menders of the text have improved, and argues at length that the eating alludes to the lustings of Israel in the desert, supporting it with a rendering that takes the word for quietness as a quail; Wesley reads the hands as those of men as wicked as himself, and glosses the eating with the remark that the wrath fell so upon Job own sons.

Henry dwells on the weight of the language, that every word speaks terror since it is not only justice but wrath, and the fury of that wrath, rained like the fire and brimstone upon Sodom, and suggests that Zophar may be reflecting on the death of Job children while they were eating and drinking.

debates.question: What does the eating allude to?
debates.positions: Clarke argues at length for the wilderness, finding a plain allusion to the lustings of Israel and the quails, supporting it with a rendering of the earlier verse that takes the word for quietness as a quail, and setting four verses beside the narrative and the psalm that retells it; Henry and Wesley hear a much more local allusion, that Zophar is reflecting on the death of Job own children while they were eating and drinking.

debates.question: Whose hands come upon him?
debates.positions: Ellicott reads them as the hands of the miserable, coming in retaliation, and mentions but doubts a second sense in which every blow that can make a man wretched shall reach him; Wesley makes them the hands of men as wicked as himself, so that his wickedness is punished by his own kind; Henry has his hand against every one and therefore every man hand against him.

outliers.view: Builds an argument from a rendering that takes the word for quietness as a quail, and sets four verses of this passage beside the narrative of the manna and the quails to show what Zophar had in view.
Suggests that the picture of wrath falling on a man just as he is about to fill his belly may be a deliberate reflection on the death of Job children while they were eating and drinking.

themes: there shall none of his meat be left
in the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits
God shall cast the fury of his wrath upon him
rain it upon him while he is eating
quails and the graves of lust

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch arrange the two verbs of the twenty-fourth verse as a conditional clause and take that to be the relation the poet intended, so that flight from the near weapon ends under the arrow of the brazen bow; Ellicott states it as a rule that if he escaped one mischance another should overtake him, takes the terrors as cumulative, and then steps outside the exposition to judge the whole as true in a sense and even a truism but utterly false in its application to Job.

Gill reads the weapon as the sword of God on Bar Tzemach authority and takes the flight itself as evidence of guilt in the conscience; he prefers the arrow drawn out of the body to Broughton drawing it from the quiver; and he gives three senses of the secret places, hiding places, God treasuries of vengeance, and the store of secret sins.

Clarke reads the verse as archery in sequence and quotes Coverdale twice, lists the different instruments God is said to employ, and alone names a precedent for the unblown fire, suspecting an allusion to the fire that fell on Korah; Wesley draws the inference from the organ named, that the mention of the gall shows the wound deep and deadly, and presses the hiding-place sense of the secret places.

debates.question: Where is the arrow drawn from?
debates.positions: Gill reports Broughton taking it of the quiver and prefers the other, that it is drawn out of the man body in the hope of curing the wound and to no purpose; Clarke reads the whole verse as archery in sequence, the arrow taken from the sheaf, discharged, piercing the vitals and passing out at the back.

debates.question: What are his secret places?
debates.positions: Gill gives three answers, the places of concealment where he promises himself safety, the store of everlasting wrath laid up among God treasuries of vengeance, and, as Ben Gersom takes it and Broughton renders it, his store of secret sins; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both take the word of hoarded goods rather than hiding places; Wesley keeps the hiding-place sense and presses it.

outliers.view: Steps outside the exposition to judge the doctrine, that all of this was perfectly true in a sense and even a truism, but utterly false in its application to Job himself.

Sharpen the clause by contrast, that where a Psalm calls God store of earthly goods for men a treasured thing, here the stores a man lays up for himself are so called, and darkness is decreed against them because they were gathered covetously and without regard to the hand that gives.

themes: he shall flee from the iron weapon
the bow of steel shall strike him through
the glittering sword cometh out of his gall
all darkness shall be hid in his secret places
a fire not blown

schools.summary: Gill offers three referents for the heaven that reveals him, God himself, the angels of heaven as the Targum takes it, and the judgments that descend from heaven, instancing the flood, the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, and destruction by thunder and lightning; and he reports from Kimchi a reading that makes the increase of the house its walls, since a dilapidation can be expressed as a pouring down of stones.

Clarke hears in both verses a further allusion to the destruction of Korah company, the heaven revealing their iniquity when the glory of the Lord appeared and the earth rising when the ground clave asunder, and presses the inference that Zophar would not have passed over such well-attested facts had he known the record; Wesley makes the heaven God as a swift witness and adds that Zophar is still reflecting on Job case and the fire that fell from heaven.

Ellicott says in one sentence that all nature combines to bring about a ruin decreed by God, and then closes the speech with an observation about the speaker, that here we take leave of Zophar, who does not reply again, having exhausted himself for all his opening boast.

debates.question: What does the heaven revealing his iniquity mean?
debates.positions: Gill offers God, the angels, or the judgments that descend from heaven, and instances the flood, Sodom and lightning; Clarke reads a specific allusion to the destruction of Korah company, with the heaven revealing their iniquity and the earth opening under them; Wesley makes it God as a swift witness and hears a reflection on the fire that fell on Job own flocks; Ellicott generalises it as all nature combining.

outliers.view: Closes the speech by noticing the speaker rather than the doctrine, that here we take leave of Zophar, who does not reply again, having exhausted himself notwithstanding the thoughts he claimed compelled him to answer.
Hears the verse as a direct thrust at Job, since the fire that fell from heaven upon his flocks is the very thing the clause about heaven revealing iniquity would call to mind.

themes: the heaven shall reveal his iniquity
the earth shall rise up against him
the increase of his house shall depart
walls that flow away
we take leave of Zophar

schools.summary: Clarke states the chapter largest claim openly, following the bishop of Killala reading of the word for quietness as a quail and holding that the poet is adorning his composition with allusions to his own people history, which fixes the date of the poem after the transgression of Israel at the graves of lust; he claims to have strengthened the reasoning by adding the manna and the rebellion of Korah, and concludes without hedging that the Book of Job is not so old as the Pentateuch; Wesley stops on the word heritage, so called to denote its stability against the inheritance got by fraud.

Gill draws the contrast that governs the whole speech, that a wicked man has his portion from God but his portion is not God himself, as a good man portion is, being at most in this life and afterwards among devils and damned spirits.

debates.question: When was the Book of Job composed?
debates.positions: Clarke argues from the alleged allusions to the quails, the manna and the rebellion of Korah that the poem must be later than the Pentateuch, and says so against those who make it older, reporting that the bishop who first noticed the quail reading has been most unmeritedly ridiculed for it; Ellicott, earlier in the same chapter, reasons from the opposite end of similar evidence, that the language about brooks of honey and butter is not precisely identical with the promise made of Canaan and may show a community of proverbial speech rather than dependence, so that the phrase need not have originated with the Pentateuch at all. Neither cites the other.

outliers.view: Defends the bishop of Killala against ridicule and stakes a date for the whole book on the reading, holding that the allusions prove the poem was composed after the events they name, a point he says has never been and never can be disproved.
Reads the second noun as chosen for its stability, the heritage being as firm as an inheritance to the right heir and set deliberately against the inheritance the man had got by fraud and violence.

themes: this is the portion of a wicked man from God
the heritage appointed unto him
a portion that is not God himself
the date of the poem
an inheritance got by fraud
